title: Finding a class file should be [[straightforward]].
hook: OneSpace is a college communication app I designed for the Microsoft Design Challenge. It gives every class one home for its conversations, files and notices.

facts.label: Role
facts.value: Research, app structure, wireframes and screen design

facts.label: Platform
facts.value: Phone app, with a smartwatch companion

facts.label: Methods
facts.value: Interviews, group discussion, survey, persona, paper wireframes

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Design concept. Not built or tested with users

summary: The problem: when college classes moved online, every teacher picked their own apps. Students had to keep up with all of them, and files and notices got lost in between.
What I did: I interviewed students and teachers, surveyed 127 people, and designed a phone app where each class has one home.
What I learned: most people (58%) did not mind using several apps. What cost them time was hunting for things. So the design is built around finding a file and catching a notice quickly.
Where it stands: a full set of screens for phone and watch. It was a design entry, so it has not been built or tested with users.

lead.alt: Five OneSpace phone screens side by side: spaces, channels, a class chat, files and announcements
lead.caption: The heart of the app, left to right: your spaces, the channels inside one, a class conversation, that class's files, and its announcements.

sections.label: The problem
sections.heading: Every teacher picked a different app

blocks.p: The challenge asked for a way to improve collaboration in India. That is a wide brief, so I picked one part of it: how colleges communicate. Classes had moved online, and each teacher was using whichever apps they were comfortable with.
For a student, that meant one class on WhatsApp, another on email and a third on Google Classroom. Keeping up was tiring. Finding something from last week was worse.

figures.alt: Diagram comparing five steps to find a timetable today with three steps in OneSpace
figures.caption: The problem in one picture. Today a student has to remember which app each teacher uses. In OneSpace the path is the same for every class.

aside.title: A limit to be clear about.
aside.detail: This was a design challenge entry. I had no college to try it in and no way to build it, so everything after the research is a design proposal.

sections.label: My plan
sections.heading: Four stages, from listening to finished screens

blocks.p: I split the work into four stages and did not start drawing screens until the third. The first two were about understanding the problem well enough to describe it in one sentence.

figures.alt: Diagram of four stages: discover, define, develop and deliver, with the work done in each
figures.caption: What I did in each stage. The problem statement was written after the research, not before it.

sections.label: Research
sections.heading: I asked people before I designed anything

blocks.p: I ran more than five one-to-one interviews with people of different ages and professions. I also held a group discussion over video with students from several colleges. Then I sent out a ten-question survey, and 127 people answered.

figures.alt: Slide from the original deck with three interview quotes, two from students and one from a teacher
figures.caption: Three things I heard. Read the teacher's quote on the right first: students were inheriting whichever apps each teacher found easiest.

blocks.p: The survey showed how scattered things were. Ten different apps were being used for the same job, and most people used several of them every day.

figures.alt: Bar chart of the apps used for institute communication, led by Google Meet at 89 percent and WhatsApp at 76 percent
figures.caption: Apps used for official communication. Google Meet, WhatsApp, email and Google Classroom were each used by more than half of the 127 people.

blocks.p: Then came the surprise. I expected people to hate using so many apps. Most did not.

figures.alt: Three small bar charts: time spent in these apps each day, how using several apps feels, and whether people would use one combined app
figures.caption: The middle chart changed my direction: 58.3% said using several apps was fine and only 14.2% found it frustrating.

blocks.p: So the real problem was smaller than I thought. People could live with many apps. What they could not do easily was find the file or the notice they needed. That became the thing to design for.

aside.title: What I chose not to assume.
aside.detail: More than half said "Yes, I might" use one combined app. I did not treat that as proof people needed one. Being willing to try something is not the same as needing it.

sections.label: Who it is for
sections.heading: One student to keep in mind

blocks.p: To keep the interviews in view while designing, I wrote a persona: one made-up student who stands for the people I spoke to. Whenever I was unsure about a screen, I asked whether it would help him.

figures.alt: Persona card for Vivek, a 20-year-old engineering student in Goa, with his situation, wants and frustrations
figures.caption: Vivek's phone is short on storage, which is why the app has a Lite mode. He finds it awkward to ask for help, which is why the screens use plain labels.

blocks.p: I boiled the research down to four problems. For each one I asked what would fix it, and that gave me six features. Parents came up in the interviews as a third group, so one feature is for them.

figures.alt: Diagram linking four problems to six features, each tagged with the problem it answers
figures.caption: Each feature on the right is tagged with the problem it answers. Nothing went into the app without a problem behind it, except the parental controls.

blocks.p: Before settling on these, I drew a mind map to explore other answers. That map is also where I decided to design for the phone first and add a watch app later.

figures.alt: Mind map from the original deck linking problems to solutions and features
figures.caption: The mind map from my deck. It runs from the problems, through possible solutions, out to specific features.

sections.label: Structure
sections.heading: A map of the app before any screens

blocks.p: Next I drew a map of everything the app would hold and how the parts connect. After logging in there are six areas: Spaces, Channels, Chat, Announcements, Profile and My Files. Admins get a few extra options in each.

figures.alt: Map of the OneSpace app showing six areas under login, each with its own actions
figures.caption: The app map from my deck. Each column is one area, with what you can do there listed below it.

blocks.p: The map also let me check the three things students do most. Each one should start from the class and take only a few taps.

figures.alt: Diagram of three tasks, find a file, catch an announcement and join a class call, each as a short path of screens
figures.caption: Three everyday tasks. Every one begins the same way: open your spaces, then pick the class.

blocks.p: I sketched every screen on paper before opening any design tool. Paper is quick to change, so I could try a layout, see what was wrong with it and redraw it in minutes.

figures.alt: Photographed paper wireframes for the OneSpace phone and watch screens
figures.caption: Paper sketches for spaces, channels, chat, announcements, files, profile, calls and the watch.

blocks.p: A student thinks "my database class", not "the app my database teacher uses". So the app starts with spaces. A space can be your college, a study group, or just you. Inside a space, channels are grouped the way a timetable is.

figures.alt: OneSpace screen listing the user's spaces as tiles with unread counts
figures.caption: Spaces. One tile for each group you belong to, with its unread count on the corner.

figures.alt: OneSpace screen listing channels grouped under Classes, Labs, Hangout and Fun
figures.caption: Channels inside a space, grouped as Classes, Labs, Hangout and Fun.

figures.alt: OneSpace chat screen for a class channel with a shared file and an announcement card
figures.caption: A class conversation, with a shared timetable and an exam notice.

figures.alt: The channels screen with five numbered notes explaining its parts
figures.caption: The channels screen, part by part.

figures.alt: The class chat screen with five numbered notes explaining its parts
figures.caption: The class conversation, part by part. Calls start from the header, so there is no need to open a separate meeting app.

sections.label: The design
sections.heading: Files and notices get their own place

blocks.p: In a chat, last week's timetable is buried under everything said since. So files and announcements each have their own screen. The chat only points to them.

figures.alt: OneSpace files screen with All and Starred tabs, sort and filter
figures.caption: Files. Tabs for All and Starred, with sort and filter, and the date each file was shared.

figures.alt: OneSpace announcements screen with General and Mentions tabs
figures.caption: Announcements. General and Mentions tabs. Upcoming items show how long is left.

figures.alt: OneSpace profile and settings screen
figures.caption: Profile and settings, including status, themes and preferences.

aside.title: The trade-off.
aside.detail: Two more screens mean a little more moving around. For this to be quicker than scrolling a chat, the default sort order and the links back to the class have to be right.

sections.label: The design
sections.heading: Made for people who find new apps hard

blocks.p: One teacher told me younger people pick up new apps quickly while she has to struggle. That stayed with me. The app had to be simple and readable first.

list: A Lite mode for phones that are short on storage.
Language support. The profile is shown here in Hindi and in French.
An accessibility setting, reminders, and adding important dates to the calendar.

figures.alt: OneSpace profile screen in Hindi
figures.caption: The profile in Hindi.

figures.alt: OneSpace profile screen in French
figures.caption: The same screen in French.

figures.alt: Four OneSpace smartwatch screens: home, a call, spaces and a chat
figures.caption: The watch app: home, a call, your spaces and a chat.

blocks.p: I also designed screens for parents and for calls.

figures.alt: OneSpace parental control screen with a usage ring and links to notes, assignments, tests and attendance
figures.caption: For parents: time spent, notes from teachers, assignments, tests and attendance.

figures.alt: OneSpace audio call screen listing speakers and guests
figures.caption: An audio call, with speakers and guests listed apart.

figures.alt: OneSpace video call screen with a shared screen above a grid of participants
figures.caption: A video call: the shared screen on top, everyone else below.

sections.label: What comes next
sections.heading: What I would do before building it

blocks.p: The design is complete, but it has not been in front of users yet. These are the next three steps I would take.

steps.title: Test three tasks.
steps.detail: Find last week's assignment, find the latest announcement and join the right class. Time each one against how students do it today.

steps.title: Start with one class.
steps.detail: Try it with a single class before a whole college, and count how long it takes the teacher to set up.

steps.title: Launch smaller.
steps.detail: The first version would be the class, its files and its announcements. Parental controls, calls and the watch app can wait until those work.

blocks.p: My deck also lists longer-term ideas: desktop apps, usability studies with more kinds of users, and trying it outside education.

sections.label: What I learned
sections.heading: Let the research change the plan

blocks.p: I started with an answer: one app for everything. The survey told me that was not what people needed most. The useful part of this project is that I listened, and the design got more focused because of it.
If I did it again, I would decide what goes in the first version straight from the research, and keep everything else for later.
